title: MRI changes in cryptococcal meningoencephalitis exacerbated by antifungal treatment due to post-infectious inflammatory syndrome: A case report
case_prompt:
A 72-year-old previously healthy woman presented with dysarthria and severe limb weakness, rendering her unable to walk independently. On examination, her temperature was 38.3°C, blood pressure 125/73 mmHg, and heart rate 93 bpm. Neurologic examination revealed moderate dysarthria, neck stiffness, and a positive Kernig’s sign; motor and sensory testing were otherwise normal. Routine blood tests showed a white blood cell count of 8.50 × 10^3/µL and a C-reactive protein level of 0.14 mg/dL. Serologic tests for HIV, HBV, HCV, HTLV-1, EBV, CMV, HSV, and syphilis were negative. Tumor markers including SCC antigen, NSE, CA19-9, CEA, and soluble IL-2 receptor were within normal limits.

Initial brain MRI demonstrated subtle meningeal enhancement in the sulci of the cerebellum and left parietal lobe on postcontrast T1-weighted images; T2-weighted, FLAIR, and diffusion-weighted sequences were unremarkable. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed 254 cells/µL, total protein 51 mg/dL, and glucose 43 mg/dL; India ink staining showed encapsulated yeast. Blood cultures later grew Cryptococcus neoformans. The patient received liposomal amphotericin B and flucytosine, with gradual clinical and CSF improvement, and was discharged.

On day 52 of antifungal therapy, she redeveloped headache, fever, and altered mental status. Repeat MRI showed new hyperintense lesions on FLAIR and T2-weighted images in the cerebellum, middle cerebellar peduncles, and left parietal lobe with associated edema, enlargement of the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle, and increased meningeal enhancement on postcontrast T1-weighted images. Repeat CSF analysis demonstrated a decrease in cryptococcal antigen titer and cell count compared with prior values, and blood and CSF cultures were negative.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Cryptococcal meningitis recurrence — “Considering the course of the disease, CM recurrence was suspected.”; excluded because “the decrease in cryptococcal antigen titers and CSF cell counts compared with the initial data, along with negative blood and CSF cultures, suggests that the second event was not caused by cryptococcal infection, but by immune-mediated mechanisms, specifically PIRS.”  
2. Primary brain tumor — considered due to new contrast-enhancing parenchymal lesions on MRI; “In the present case, the differential diagnoses included primary brain tumor and brain metastasis in addition to CM exacerbation.”  
3. Brain metastasis — considered due to the appearance of new enhancing lesions on MRI; “In the present case, the differential diagnoses included primary brain tumor and brain metastasis in addition to CM exacerbation.”  
4. Postinfectious inflammatory response syndrome (PIRS) — considered when imaging and clinical symptoms worsened despite laboratory improvements; “The symptoms and imaging exacerbations, despite improvement in laboratory data, were considered immune-mediated delayed exacerbations, known as postinfectious inflammatory response syndrome (PIIRS), rather than a recurrence.”
